lines.text: You'll be off up the Reach, then. I drove cattle up there. Through the old gate, down past the mill, and there was never any call to move it that I saw.

Grass does well up there. Always has. Which is — anyway. Skir come over the hedge at dusk hunting Nibbin out of the tussock. I watched one drop, come up with nothing, go up, and drop again twenty foot along.
Mind the gate on your way through. The far latch drops if you don't lift it, and the one down past the mill was the better gate anyway, only they
The Reach has come up green right down to the fence line.
Tolm will get a crop off his west side in a year like this. His father had that field in oats. Or barley — it was one of the two. Tolm put it down to grass the day he took it on.
The Reach is short this year. I'd have had the beasts down off that rise a month early.
The town fields go the way the Reach goes and Tolm's west side goes first. It went first the year of the wet harvest and all, and that was years before ever he touched the drainage down at that end.
Maren let me hold the survey book and I looked at every page of it and there isn't a single drawing anywhere in the whole thing.
My da says I'm not to keep on at her about it. I'm going to, though.
There's a Nibbin under the mill step and her name is Kettle, and I told Maren her name was Kettle and she wrote her in as a Nibbin and Kettle isn't in the book anywhere at all.
Kettle's gone white round the face.
She's the same one and I'd know her anywhere and Maren wrote her in again at the turn and it still only says Nibbin. I'm learning my letters. There's a white bit down the side of the page.
West gate's down again. Bramblehog, same post. Back up before dark.
Loamunder go along under the west field all night. I've ploughed it top and bottom and never turned one up.
Six weeks to harvest and dry all week. Two hands, four fields.
A track's the easy sign. A browse line takes longer. It's where something's come along and eaten the tips off a bush and left the stems standing, and the bush is still stood there, mind. With me?
The stems are what I measure. A folding rule, notched down the side, off my mother.

Scrapes now. A scrape is bark rubbed off. Dug is different. Dug leaves a cast, which is to say a little heap thrown out at the side of it. Seen one? Pollywisp you'll not see till the spring. Rest of the year they're down in the wet.
Post's out of the ground down the west end. Whole post, root and all.
Something comes through the wire there and takes it away with it. Cart gets to the second stile and I carry the rest from there, so that's a morning gone before I've started on anything.
Warden wants a number off me. I showed her the post. She wrote something down.
The best week of my year, this. Third year I've come up for the picking.
The grass is four or five days further on than the same week last year, and the tussock's crept north on me as well. A hundred paces from the old edge to the new.
Wet springs, that'll be. There's an antler stone up on the north rise and it's where I stop for my dinner.
I walked the whole tussock this morning and turned up two Nibbin, and last year I'd have seen a dozen of them before I got as far as the gate.
The Skir are still about. They're over the far hedge these days. Somebody else's ground now.
I've not picked the Reach this thick before. Knee-high on the north rise.
The same week last year it was no higher than my boot. The Nibbin have grazed that rise all week and there's grass standing yet. A Bramblehog on the path this morning hardly troubled to move for me.
Lanterns are up on the green. When the season's out the year goes over with it.

Every beast on the place gets a year older at the turn, whether it's been out on the grass all year or shut in the byre since spring. We brought ours down off the Reach the fortnight before, the way we always did.
Three posts down the west end won't hold now. I pack stone round them.
Put them back in the holes I dug six years ago. Ground's gone soft at that end. They'll not hold another winter.
The tussock's six hundred paces north of where I picked my first year. I pace it the same week every year.

Six years of the same four miles, and the Nibbin graze that rise flatter every year of it. Wet springs, I'd have said, and I only see it the one week. Picking's better than it ever was. Two more baskets in that rise before dark.
